Does the Canadian government elevator buy or purchase screening shutouts, or, in other wo'ds, the dockage of 3 per cent or over on grain that is unloaded, in their Port Arthur plant, or does the Canadian government elevator only handle for its own account the dockage on grain that is allowed the terminal elevator, according to its tariff?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mr. LAPOINTE (For the Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
The procedure followed is that when cars of grain are unloaded 
into the Canadian Government elevator at Port Arthur, warehouse receipts, both for grain and screenings, outturns showing charges, and official weight, certificates are sent to the Winnipeg office of the Canadian Government elevator system, where they are delivered to the party surrendering the bills of lading, usually the commission merchant acting as agent for the shipper. If these parties desire to dispose of the warehouse receipts for screenings to the Canadian Government elevator, the manager of the Winnipeg office is always prepared to purchase same at the current market price, and is provided with a fund, designated "Special Account," from which to make payment for such purchases. The holder of warehouse receipts for screenings is under absolutely no obligation to dispose of same to the Canadian Government elevator, but is always at liberty to take delivery of the documents and dispose of same to the best possible advantage or in any manner he may see fit.

1.	Has the portion within the city of Toronto of the Toronto and Suburban Railway been offered for sale to the city, and on what terms, either by the government or National Railways?
2.	Have the bondholders objected to the sale of a part instead of the whole road, and can the sale of a part be legally consummated?
3.	Have the bondholders notified the government to this effect, and how does the sale now stand?

1.	The Toronto Suburban Company's lines within the city of Toronto are governed by a franchise granted by the former town of Toronto Junction (now Ward 7 of the city of Toronto), which expired in 1921. Under their franchise, the former town of Toronto Junction, or its successors, had the right, upon notice, to take over the whole of the lines within the limits of the town at a valuation to be agreed upon, and fixed by arbitration. The city of Toronto duly gave notice in 1921 of its intention to take over th^ franchise lines, and a tentative valuation was made between the two parties, which has not yet been acted upon.
2.	An objection was made on behalf of the bondholders that the whole of the lines of the Suburban Company, both inside and outside of the franchise limits, had to be taken by the city on the expiry of the franchise, but tills objection was not concurred in by the Toronto Suburban Railway Company, and is not maintainable. The bondholders are subject to the franchise terms to the same extent as

Questions
the railway company, and while objection may be made, at discretion, by the bondholders to the sale of lines, or parts of lines outside the franchise limits, within the franchise limits the consummation of the sale or taking over by the city depends only upon the fixing of the consideration to be paid.
3.	The representatives of the bondholders claim that they must be consulted and must agree to any value fixed or to any disposal of lines outside the franchise limits. In the correctness of this position the railway company concurs. The terms and the extent of the taking over are now under active consideration by the parties concerned, subject to the rights of the bondholders as stated.

On section 2-Definition "combine:"

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I mentioned
my intention to strike out the words "in the opinion of the registrar or any commissioner" after the word "as" in line 9. I offer that

speechtext:
The amendment is

The amendment is all right, but I suggest to the Prime Minister to alter the words "or are likely to operate," and insert in place thereof the words"or are about to operate."
A combine likely to operate is something intangible, whereas a combine about to opera: means one that has been formed, in which case there might be something tangible for the registrar to get at as being improper.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The words
"or are likely to operate" are taken from section 2, subsection 1. of the Combines and Fair Prices Act of 1919, and I imagine that they were chosen with care at the time. I
Combines

fail to see very much distinction between the words "likely to" and "about to." I think the words "likely to" indicate the probability, and that is what should be aimed at for the purpose of investigation.

Suppose that two concerns were about to get together and make their financial arrangements, and six persons, under the following section of the act, came along and said, "Oh, this concern is likely to operate as a combine, we will put a stop to it and put an end to the financial arrangement," whereas, if those two concerns had got together in such a way that there was a tangible evidence that a combine would occur, it would mean that the registrar would have some facts to go on, so that he could actually prosecute under the act. 1 am quite aware that these words are taken from the Combines and Fair Prices Act, but under that act I think the complaint had to be made in such a case to a judge. I am speaking from memory in that regard. I suggest to the minister that the words "are about to operate" indicate something tangible, something fixed, and the words "likely to operate" indicate something intangible or something not fixed, but something which might likely take place in the future.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not see very much force in what my non. friend has said. I cannot see that the use of the word "about" will alter materially what is aimed at. If it will help to reconcile my hon. friend to the section as a whole, I have no objection, if he likes to move the amendment, to have it adopted.

I think it would be a misfortune to change the word "likely" to the word "about." An ounce of prevention is surely worth a pound of cure, and if, as the hon. member indicates, two concerns are likely to be brought into a combination or a merger to the extent that they might, as a result, by being brought into combination, be likely to operate to the detriment of the public, the ounce of prevention is what should be used if anything is to be used, and prevention of that particular combine, if that were brought about, could be made effective. We should not wait until they have been brought together and consolidated and had a free field to see if they could evade the intention of the law. Personally, I do not think my hon. friend has anything whatever to fear. It would certainly suggest discredit on the entire intent of the act to make any such change as that, for the reason which has been given.

I can hardly follow the reasoning of the Minister of Labour. I quite realize the intent of the act. I said that I realized the intent of the act, and I voted for it. But I certainly think, as the bill now stands, to have something tangible is a great deal better than to have something intangible, and I cannot see how the amendment which I suggested to the Prime Minister does any harm, to the bill itself. I do not think the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) caught the drift of my remarks.

I should like to say a word in connection with a statement made in this House by two hon. members on this side regarding an alleged fruit combine in British Columbia. I want to state definitely that no such thing as a fruit combine exists in British Columbia. There is in British Columbia an organization that is trying to get what it produces to the consumer with the least possible expense. In days gone by, certain profiteers were making as high as a dollar or a dollar and a quarter a box on fruit, whereas the people producing this fruit in British Columbia were getting only from 7 cents to SI .25 per box for raising, packing and shipping, and they did not think that was right. They have formed an organization so that they will be able to give the consumer on the prairies and in other places the best possible prices on fruit.
In connection with the bill before the committee, I should like to make one or two suggestions, and the first one is in regard to the six persons who will lay a complaint against any combine. The registrar should see that those six persons are not from any one company or concern. It would be very easy for a concern that was running in opposition to another to have six of its members lay a complaint; in fact, this would be a sort of blackmail. The law should be such that those six persons should be from six separate concerns, and when they lay a complaint, the first thing the registrar should do would be to call upon them to prove the allegation laid before him, and if need be, he should put them under oath and make them prove it. This is only reasonable. In the next place, those who do the investigating should be sworn to secrecy. They should not be at liberty to make public in any way what they may find until such time as the matter comes before the court.

l intimated
also another amendment that I would ask to have inserted with respect to this clause. The amendment is to the effect of lequiring the application for an investigation to be made by six persons, British subjects, resident in Canada. I beg to move:

I should be glad to have an explanation why the benefits of this law should be restricted to British subjects. I think it is the sentiment and tradition amongst our people that any person domiciled in Canada should be protected in the exercise of his legal rights and should have free recourse to the courts. There are some jurisdictions, for instance, where aliens are not allowed to hold real estate. I think that is the case in
the state of New York; but that has not been the case, so far as I am aware, in any province qf Canada, and I do not see that the bill is in any way improved by restricting the class of persons who may make a complaint. Take, for instance, the case of a citizen of the United States, whose business has brought him to Canada, who has lived here for many years, whose interests are here, but who, through sentimental or other reasons, has hopes in his old age to return to the United States and who has never ceased to be a citizen of that country. Why should such a man as that be precluded from laying a complaint under this law? I see no reason for the change, though, perhaps, the Prime Minister, who is in charge of the bill, may have some weighty reasons which may show me that I am wrong in my view. The principle I would lay down is this, that this is in the nature of a judicial inquiry, and the courts are and should be open to all dwellers in this land who are behaving themselves in a seemly fashion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The clause as originally drafted stated that any person resident in Canada might make an application for an investigation. That was thought to be too broad, and for that reason the words "six persons" were substituted. The addition of the words "British subjects" was simply to ensure a little more care as to putting this legislation into operation. As my hon. friend knows, there are large numbers of foreigners who are domiciled in Canada, who are not wholly familiar with our laws, institutions, and methods of proceeding, and it is conceivable that, for reasons more of agitation than otherwise, some of them might be persuaded to endeavour to set this particular law in motion simply because it is so easy for the individual to do so. I should think, if any six persons in the country who are not British subjects, really had ground for believing that a combine existed which was operating in restraint of trade or to the detriment of the public, they would find very little difficulty in securing six other citizens who were British subjects to make the application on their behalf. I do not believe it will really affect the freedom, the liberty or the right of anyone in any material significance, and if it tends to give a sense of greater security to some of those who fear that there is too much latitude in the law as it stands, I think it is advisable to retain the words "British subject."

If the Prime Minister has no objection, I would suggest that in line 11

I suggest further that the section be amended to read:
The application shall be accompanied by a sworn statement showing, etc.
As the section stands, a mere statement, without any qualification, is required.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am prepared to be governed by the wishes of the committee in this particular, but I do not think we should make it difficult for an application to be submitted. The purpose of the legislation is to give to the citizens of the country a feeling of assurance that there is an avenue of approach against any possible injustice, and to make that approach as easy as possible. The registrar would have to be satisfied himself that the application put before him was one deserving of that careful consideration which the law would expect, and one that merited an investigation, before anything further could be done. The fact that the application must be sworn to might make it more difficult for some persons to apply. If however the committee thinks that the suggested change is advisable I shall be prepared to consider it, but I rather hesitate to compel people who are not accustomed to taking oaths to submit to such an obligation in a matter of this kind. I should be glad to have an expression of opinion from the committee.
A statement over the signature of six persons is definite enough without being sworn to.

The amendment my hon. friend proposes might, I think, be out of joint with subsection (a) of section 17 which gives the registrar or any commissioner power to exact an affidavit or a written affirmation at any stage of the proceedings.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 6-Registrar shall cause inquiry to be made:

It might be well, if the Prime Minister sees no objection to the proposal, to have this section amended in accordance with a provision in the Immigration Act which I shall read to the committee.

The hearing of all cases brought before such board of inquiry shall be separate and apart from the public, but in the presence of the immigrant, passenger or other person concerned whenever practicable, and such immigrant, passenger or other person shall have the right to be represented by counsel whenever any evidence or testimony touching the case is received by the board.
I think that the accused should have the right to be represented by counsel whenever any evidence or testimony touching the case is received by the registrar, and that he should have the right to adduce evidence on his own behalf. A similar privilege is accorded immigrants who come into the country and in regard to whom the question of deportation is under consideration. If we do this much for persons who are not citizens, surely we can give a citizen accused under this legislation the right to be present and to be represented by counsel. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The point of view which my hon. friend presents suggests that the persons complained against as belonging to a combine that is operating to the dertiment of the public are in the position of defendants or accused. I think that is a wholly erroneous assumption. The fact that a representation is made by six persons that some particular concern is a combine operating to the detriment of the public does not place the persons involved in that alleged combine in the position of defendants or accused until, after an investigation by the registrar and after an investigation by the commissioner, and at the instance of the attorney general of the province or the Solicitor General of the Dominion, they are brought into court as having violated a section of the act which we shall discuss later. At that stage it would be quite proper that the persons about to be placed on trial should have the right to be represented by counsel and have all the protection that the law can give them. But for the purpose of a preliminary inquiry to ascertain whether there are prima facie reasons for believing that a combine exists and is operating to the detriment of the public, I think that the more freedom that is left to the registrar to make that preliminary investigation, the better. It goes without saying that the first act of the registrar would be to bring

Combines
before him the persons against whom the particular complaint is directed. It is conceivable that some of the applications might on the face of them be of such a character that he would dismiss them without going thus far, that is to say, if they were frivolous or vexatious. On the other hand, I cannot conceive of an investigation proceeding a single stage without the registrar getting immediately into touch with the persons against whom the complaint is made. I do not think it would be wise to introduce the lawyers at that early stage of the proceedings.
I was not speaking on behalf of the lawyers.

Is the Prime Minister of opinion that the registrar has to be satisfied with the prima facie proof adduced, or does he think that it is imperative that he make an inquiry whether or not he is satisfied with that preliminary proof? It does seem to me, from a reading of the action, that the registrar is bound to make an inquiry into the matter, or have the commissioner make the inquiry, whether he is satisfied or not with the preliminary proof adduced. That is the point I raised a day or so ago. I said that if the registrar had any shadow of proof before him-I, did not care what the proof of the six persons was-then there was no objection to his proceeding to investigate any business. But I did think it was a mistake to make it incumbent on the registrar to examine into a business before he was satisfied in the initial stages that there was something wrong. If the Prime Minister would consider that point I should be glad to have his opinion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think the registrar must proceed up to the point where he is satisfied that either the complaint is frivolous or vexatious and without sufficient foundation or that there is substantial ground for believing that the representations are accurate. It should be left to the discretion of the registrar to proceed in the matter so far as satisfying himself one way or the other. That is all that the section requires. It does not propose that the registrar shall start a full-fledged investigation involving wide and extensive examinations if on the face of things there appears no ground for anything of the kind. On the other hand, if the application does contain representations which make it advisable for the registrar to go pretty carefully into the case before reporting to the minister, he will doubtless proceed as far as the circumstances seem to warrant.

Is it not the case in the opinion of the right hon. gentleman that the
registrar under this section would have to investigate the books of the concern or make such reasonable inquiry to establish whether or not the complaint was vexatious or not? How could he determine otherwise? The point I am drawing to the attention of the right hon. gentleman is this, that after the word "registrar" in the second line a few words should be inserted to show that after sufficient proof had been adduced to the satisfaction of the registrar he would proceed to make an investigation. As the section now stands I think the registrar has no option but to make an investigation to determine whether the complaint is frivolous or not.

But the responsibility is his to say that he has looked into the matter and found that there are not reasonable grounds for believing that the combine is operating to the detriment of the public. In that case the registrar would be bound to make an investigation, which might be of considerable extent, to determine whether the allegations made were frivolous or not. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think, Mr. Chairman, if my hon. friends will look at the next section they will see pretty clearly by the very first words what is intended:
If after such inquiry as he deems the circumstances warrant, the registrar is of the opinion that the
application is frivolous or vexatious,-
That is the extent to which the registrar is expected to go. He must satisfy his own mind having regard to the circumstances, and the inquiry that he is to make is clearly such inquiry as he deems the circumstances warrant. That is the whole purpose of the section.

I think the Prime Minister is thinking of the second inquiry. I am speaking of the preliminary inquiry. That [DOT]is the only one I have ever taken exception to. I have not taken exception to the second inquiry at all. If the registrar is satisfied by the preliminary inquiry that there is a combine, an injury being done, I have never said that he should not go on. I think he should. I am entirely in accord with the Prime Minister's viewpoint there. But the one point I have made, as has been stressed a few moments ago is, notwithstanding what my hon. friend the Minister of Labour says, that section 6 makes it absolutely imperative for the registrar to make an inquiry. The Prime Minister, a few moments ago asked, if you were a registrar what would you do? I would have absolutely no alternative but to go into the combines themselves and make an investigation of these facts to find out whether the allegations and the complaints made were frivolous or not. However, I have spoken long enough on this subject.

I agree entirely with my hon friend (Mr. Marler). I think reference to section 6 will show that there are three things contemplated by that section. The first is the inquiry to be made by the registrar upon receipt of application. Secondly, the registrar himself if he has reason to believe a combine exists can start an inquiry of his own accord, and thirdly, the minister if he sees fit, can set the. machinery in motion. I do
not think the lines referred to by the Minister of Labour "or whenever the registrar shall have reason to believe" are coupled at all with the first line. He seems to think that when the application is received the registrar pauses to consider, and after doing some considering, if he thinks there is reason to believe a combine exists, he proceeds. I think the minister is reading it entirely wrong. It is perfectly obvious that there are three distinct provisions. If I am wrong in that I would suggest to the Prime Minister that he should consider an amendment to the section, for certainly it is open to that construction without any doubt. Let us read it again:
Whenever such application shall be made to the registrar-
That is one thing. Then he must proceed to make the inquiry referred to, and furthermore he may require returns to be made under oath and so on. That is one thing. Next comes this:
-whenever the registrar shall have reason to believe that a combine exists or is being formed-
He may set the law in motion. Or third, the minister may set the law in motion. If that is not the intention I would respectfully suggest that the Prime Minister had better reframc the section for I feel certain that the language is not capable of any other interpretation.

It has been suggested to me-it is not my own suggestion-that after the word "registrar" instead of the word "or" the word "and" be used. The section would then read:
Whenever such application shall be made to the registrar, and whenever the registrar shall have reason to believe that a combine exists or is being formed, etc.

Does not that go further than the hon. member intends? That would shut off any initiative on the part of the registrar, and I do not think that he means to go as far as that. Of course, the real trouble about this bill is that those who are chiefly in favour of it have not taken the time to find out what it does mean. The hon. Minister of Labour is just as right in his contentions on this clause as he has been in the whole of his main argument. He is keeping up his batting average. He is one hundred ' per cent wrong exactly, no more and no less. I do not know that it makes very much difference. After all, this is only a start. The government are satisfied with the bill; let them have it. They think it is all right; let them have it. We have tried to point out how absurd these things are, but they do not want

any assistance, none at all, so why should we delay the proceedings one way or the other. Of course, if English means what English is supposed to mean, if these written words are to be taken not as a joke from the Department of Labour but as meaning just exactly what they are supposed to mean, the hon. gentleman who has raised this point is absolutely right.
I want to ask a further question. Can my right hon. friend give us any light as to what the words "or others" mean in this same section? I admit we have had one explanation from the Minister of Labour, and 1 must congratulate him upon that. In that explanation he again kept up his batting average. I think his explanation was again one hundred per cent error, because he tells us that the reason that the words "or others" are put in there is this, that these eombinesters sometimes are so clever that they can take the position that they are neither producers nor consumers, and they therefore are "others," so that the word "others" according to the minister means them.
The hon. gentleman is misquoting me, as he will find if he refers to the record.

We will see just what he says. Here it is:
It came to my attention some two or three years ago that these words "or others'' were very necessary on account of the business in which such "eombinesters" were engaged, that if these words "or others" were not there, they would be able, with legal advice, to prove conclusively that they were neither a producer of the thing they were combined to deal in. nor a consumer of that particular thing, and that therefore, the words "or others" were necessary there to include them and every citizen of this Dominion.
Now my hon. friend will say that the word "others," is put in because these people that are eombinesters can say: We are neither producers nor consumers. Perhaps I had better pause here to ask the minister if I did not read his statement right.
That part of it which you read I think was read right.

That is the only thing I am referring to, that and nothing else. My hon. friend will say that the word "others" there is put in for the purpose of protecting these wicked people from themselves. They may say they are not producers, or they may say that they are not consumers. They are in a combine and that combine may be hurting themselves, and that is the reason the word "others" is in there. That is the explanation given. I am quite sure that my right hon. friend will say that that is not his reason,

but that is the only reason we have been given up to date. I think we should be given some sane, logical reason as to why the word "others" is there.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think I can give my hon. friend a reason that he will accept. He himself is partly responsible for the insertion of those words, and I think that reason was given and given by the Minister of Labour yesterday. My hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) has only to ask his own leader and to consider what he did when he was a member of the government to discover where those words came from. I have in front of me the Combines and Fair Prices Act of 1919, which was passed when my hon. friend was a member of the government, and the language of that act is as follows:
The expression "combine" is used in this act with intended relation to articles of commerce, and it shall be deemed to have reference only to such combines, immediately hereinafter defined, as, with relation as aforesaid, have, in the opinion of the Board of Commerce of Canada (or of a single member thereof acting under authority of and for the purposes of section eight of this act) operated, or are likely to operate, to the detriment of or against the interest of the public, consumers, producers or others-
That is the language that my hon. friend was responsible for putting in the statute which was passed relating to combines. The present administration is seeking to take from previous legislation what was best and most effective in it and omit what seemed to be superfluous and unnecessary, and therefore retains those words. I confess I did not see that they had any great significance until 1 heard the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Baxter) yesterday draw the attention of the House to the fact-or rather ask the question -*was an insurance company a consumer or producer, was a transportation company a consumer or producer. He said he could not tell. Well, the purpose of this bill is to protect any section of the public, whether transportation companies, insurance companies, or anyone else. That is the reason why the words "or others" are inserted there and should be kept there. I hope my hon. friend will feel that, inasmuch as he has been partly responsible for the insertion of these words in a similar enactment perhaps there is great wisdom in their being included there.
As to the other point which has just been mentioned, let me say to my hon. friend that when he intimates the government is not anxious to receive any assistance that can be given he is quite in error, the government will welcome any assistance. What the government hopes will be avoided is unnecessary criticism, obstruction simply for the purpose

of obstruction. Nothing of the kind has been shown. But I would certainly like my hon friend and every member of the House to feel, that the government will welcome any suggestion, any assistance in making this bill as perfect as it can be made. It is a very difficult question and will require all the expert advice it is possible to offer.
Just before I leave the section we are referring to let me read the provisions one by one. First of all there is this provision:
Whenever such application shall be made to the registrar-
That is the first condition if one wishes to put it so. Then:
-or whenever the registrar shall have reason to believe that a combine exists or is being formed-
That is the second.
-or whenever so directed by the minister-
That is the third. Now continuing-
-the registrar shall cause an inquiry to be made-
I think that is, perhaps, where the fear of hon. members arises. They have a fear of the word "inquiry," they attach to it a significance which the rest of the language of the section does not justify. "Cause an inquiry to be made" does not mean that the registrar shall institute a large and extensive inquiry, going into all the business transactions of a company in a formal manner. If one reads the rest of the section one will see what is meant. Let me continue:
-cause an inquiry to be made into all such matters whether of fact or of law with respect to the said alleged combine as he shall consider necessary-
The whole of it is limited by what the registrar himself shall consider necessary to inquire into with a view of determining whether a combine exists. He is not expected to go and find out how far the combine could operate; and by the word "combine" there, reference, of course, is to a combine as defined by the act which is a combine operating to the detriment of the public. He proceeds to inquire with a view to determining whether a combine operating to the detriment of the public exists or not. Now the very next section, which still refers to the registrar says:
It, after suoli inquiry as he deems the circumstances warrant, the registrar is of the opinion that the application is frivolous or vexatious, or does not justify further inquiry he shall make a report in writing to the minister setting out the application, the statement or statements, the inquiry made and the information obtained, and his conclusions.
It is perfectly clear that the whole purpose of the section is simply to appoint some person who will receive applications and whose duty it will be to act in much the same manner
as a grand jury acts in regard to matters that are drawn to its attention to discover whether there are grounds sufficient to merit an inquiry of a more elaborate character being gone into. I think if my hon. friend will read the two sections just as they are in plain English he will find it difficult to come to any other conclusion.

It is quite true that the words in question can be found somewhere else, but I apprehend the draftsman had some reason for what he was doing, There is a good deal of difference between two acts. Words and definitions, and the like, change as acts or as objects change. That I think the right hon. gentleman must know. It is perfectly idle to say to me that I should know all about it, for frankly I do not. I thought this was really the hobby of my right hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King). I thought he would know the use of every single word in this bill. I am very much surprised to learn that instead of knowing anything about it he simply says "We have gone through your ^legislation and we have taken all the good we can find in it, dropping the unnecessary clauses." That is discarding the most ingenious although highly fallacious explanation given by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock). The Prime Minister is driven to this point, that knowing nothing about it and having no other reason to offer, he is forced to accept a suggestion made by this side of the House. Well, I think, perhaps, we shall have to let it go at that.
I would draw my hon. friend's attention to the fact that the Minister of Labour on 27th January, 1920, knew entirely too much to suit my hon. friend about these things.

We have had so many funny things-and they generally come from the same funny source-they are coming along from time to time. I do not know what my hon. friend is referring to. He is a creator of jokes as well as a great investigator.

I understand from the tenor of the right hon. mfember's speech on this matter, that the registrar would be appointed as a guardian of the rights of the public. The history of the guardians of the public is instructive. The guardian of the rights of the public unfoirtunately occupies a delicate position. Originally guaidians were instituted with human motives in regard to the rights of the poor, but. eventually they degenerated into guardians of the taxpayers, and were always on their guard against the encroachments of the poor. If this registrar is simply placed there to take the buffet and absorb the shock of public complaint ere it reaches the foot of the throne, I do not think there is very much in this legislation after all, and I would very much prefer that this registrar were given certain police powers, powers of surveillance, so that his

spare time might be employed on behalf of the people as agaiDst their would-be exploiters. My prophecy is that unless that is done his position will degenerate into that of a guardian of the exploiters of the people, and will not maintain its original intention of being a guardian of the people themselves.
I offer that as a criticism of this bill. It is all right to be precise and exact about the incidentals, but when you come to define the functions of the man or the person who is to carry out the law you are touching its nerve. Therein lies the whole work. The registrar, whoever he may be, will be exposed to much influence from the public. Any motion that comes from the public will be now and then and here and there, scattered and pretty much ineffective. It will not be concerted. The powers that will move upon him from above will not be of that kind. They will be concerted, concentrated; and woe to the man if his duties are not defined and if those duties are not so defined as to make it beyond any peradventure that he is placed there on behalf of the public. I wish the committee to note that that was the sole motive for introducing this legislation-that the public should be safeguarded from this menace that exists from growing combines. The whole intention of the legislation is defeated to begin with if you do not so state-put it in the bond-that this registrar is placed there purely for public reasons, for the public benefit, and not in any way to absorb the effect of public complaint before it reaches the point where it can be effectively heard.

speechtext:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend may have noticed that the bill gives power to the government to name some individual who already holds a position in the public service to act as registrar or, if the circumstances seem to necessitate it, to make a separate appointment; and I should think that for the class of wo:k expected of the registrar, and having regard to the character of the man who would fill the position he would correspond very nearly to a deputy minister and the salary would be proportionate. friend has in mind is an amount between $20 and $40?

speechtext: On a basis similar to other members of the Civil Service.

Does the Prime Minister really think that the registrar in this position, with the powers he has under the act, if it does not become a dead letter, should be a creature of the government, subject to dismissal at any time by the government? Should he not be in the position of members of the Civil Service Commission, or of the Railway Commission, or of the late Board of Commerce?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think it is very desirable that whoever is appointed should feel that there is some certainty of permanency about the position so long as his duties are being performed in a satisfactory manner, and I should hope that if the government ever changed, the government succeeding would retain in office whomsoever might be appointed provided he filled the office satisfactorily. I do not know that the expression "r nature of the government" is wholly a proper one to use in reference to an appointment of this kind. I think the

government would be fully aware of its responsibility to the public and to parliament in the matter of such an appointment and would seek to appoint someone whose standing in the community commended itself to the people. The government would be the first to recognize that the effect of a measure of this kind wou'd depend on the character of the men who had to do with its administration.

That does not answer my point. If 'what the Prime Minister says is right and applies generally, then judges should be appointed on the same basis. If the government can always be relied on never to dismiss anyone for selfish reasons, if the government is always of the nature depicted by some hon. gentlemen yesterday-virtuous and right no matter what issues from it-then, of course, the Prime Minister's position is defensible. But, judging from some appointments that this government has made if one may not judge from anything else, I must say that my faith in that regard has been rudely shattered.
Did you ever have faith in this government?
I can say that I have had more than I have now.
Your government made mistakes, too.

We appointed strong Liberals, and I do not know that we ever made a greater mistake than that relating to the hon. gentleman who interrupted me. If I am ever forgiven for that I shall be safe for all time. Now, I do not myself anticipate- I give my opinion for what it is worth, of course-that this registrar will have very much to do. He will have one job a month; about the end of each month he will have a small task. He may possibly have a little w-ork in between if the act is put into operation and does not become a dead letter; but practically speaking he will have one job a month. If these great inquiries that are supposed to take place are to be of the nature of the sun that dispels thieves and robbers and unworthy things, according to King Richard II in Shakespeare, if these inquiries are to act as a sun to clear away the germs that the	Prime	Minister mentioned yesterday, there will have, of course, to be an operation of the act. But the registrar sitting in his office will not be any such sun. Anyone who suggests, for example, that the Combines Investigation Act operated as a preventive must have a great imagination.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There was a registrar under the Combines Investigation Act.
He had a fine sinecure.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He was a deputy minister.

He did no work at all. The power of investigation was in the old act, but so far as that act proved a preventive of combines, it might as well have never been passed, and the whole country knows it. There were never as many combines formed in the history of Canada in the same period as during the existence of that act. My anticipation is that this will be just the same and that the registrar will have the duty of drawing his salary once a month. To the extent that it operates the act may prove vexatious, but it will get nowhere. But in the exercise of his duties, in order that at least the minimum of harm may be done and that effective action may be possible, the registrar should not be subject to dismissal at the will of the government. If such is the case he is disrobed of all judicial clothing whatsoever; there is nothing judicial about his office; he is simply there to carry out the will of the minister and of the government, subject to dismissal if he does not. The moment you place a man in a judicial position you must place him beyond the power of dismissal at the hands of the government. Is there anything of the nature of a judicial office in the post of registrar? If there is, then he should not be subject to dismissal.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I agree with my right hon. friend, I think whoever holds this position should feel that he is to all intents and purposes precisely in the same position in relation to the government as is a judge. But the duties are somewhat new and it may be that it would be difficult to find a man of experience to fill the position. Therefore I think it would not be wise to provide in the statute that the registrar shall not be removable from office until it is seen just how far it may be possible to secure a person who will fill this position in the most satisfactory manner. Personally I would not have any objection whatever to having the statute include a clause to the effect that the registrar shall be in the same position as a judge and be appointed for life; but when we are introducing legislation of a new character I think it is wise not to finally close the door to a possible change in the event of an appointment being made which would not be all that the government hoped it would be. I certainly agree that if the office were made in
Combined
any sense political it would be a great abuse of the whole purpose of the statute.
I do not know whether what I am about to offer is a practical suggestion, but would it not be possible to make the appointee responsible to parliament?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: All members ot the service in one sense are responsible to parliament.
I know.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Every minister is responsible to parliament.
But could not the appointee be removed by action of the whole House?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That practically comes to just what my right hon. friend is suggesting, that the position be similar to that of a judge. If the committee think it wise I would have no objection to this being done, but I submit that perhaps it would be better to have the registrar appointed on the understanding that his office would be a life appointment, unless after he had exercised the functions of the 5 p.m. office for some months it was found he was not the person adapted to such a position. I think it would be better to leave the door open in this way so that if the man appointed in the first instance did not measure up to what was expected of him he could be removed from office.

I suppose the appointment of a registrar would involve also the appointment of a secretary and a stenographer and provision for special office accommodation, all of w'hich would cost not less than ten or fifteen thousand dollars. Does not the Prime Minister think that before the country is saddled with any such permanent expenditure there should be some certainty of the registrar having something to do? As my right hon. leader said, I do not think the appointee will be very busy. If he has four or five investigations to make in a year I venture to say that is the utmost he will be called upon to undertake, in fact there may not be as many. Supposing we are right, if the office is once established we are committed to this expenditure. I would suggest that an officer of one of the courts in Ottawa should receive this appointment, at the outset at all events, until we see where this legislation is going to land us. Of course, he should get fair remuneration for an}' work he does. After a year, or at the outside two years, we will have an idea as to whether there is any real need for such an officer or not. There is power in the bill now to appoint some person

who already holds office. That is what I would suggest at the outset, say the registrar of one of our courts in Ottawa, or possibly the deputy minister could for the time being fill the office. There is certainly no good reason to make a life appointment and incur this heavy expenditure until we know just what the duties of registrar will involve. For my part if we find there is necessity for a registrar and important work for him to do, I certainly agree that he should not be subject to removal by any government, but should be in the same position, as a judge and be removable from office only for proper cause.

In any event I would suggest to the Prime Minister that such a life appointment be not made until it is determined that this measure is within the competency of parliament to enact. One of the most learned counsel in Toronto has already expressed the opinion that such legislation is beyond the competence of this parliament, and I for one would think that it was not in the interests of the country to appoint a registrar and staff, involving superannuation allowance and other burdens, until it is beyond doubt that this legislation is not ultra vires. Mr. Chairman, I think the question asked by the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Boys) as to whether there is any-need of a registrar being appointed is easily answered. In my opinion there is sufficient evidence before the committee now to warrant the speedy appointment of a registrar.
The other day the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) inquired as to whether the refusal by the Canadian Press Limited

as it then was-of a franchise to the proposed Ottawa paper would come within the provisions of this measure. In attempting to give some information the other evening I recited part of the history of a case that had come before the Canadian Press Limited. My remarks called forth from the Ottawa Journal two full columns of personal abuse and a double column editorial this morning. In the latter the Journal calls me almost everything that it is possible to call a man, but I suppose hon. members are not interested in such personal abuse heaped upon themselves. However, as I am termed a company promoter by the writer of the editorial, I may at once state that I never owned a share of promotion stock in my life or drew a fee for promoting a company. I am also charged with the crime of writing a letter to the Canadian Press, Limited, in stationery that happened to be bwned by a company in the city of Detroit
I Mr. Boys.]	*
of which I am president. Of course, this may be a crime in the eyes of the Ottawa Journal.
But perhaps the real reason for these abusive articles is that the managing director of the Ottawa Journal is the president of the Canadian Press which I suggested might be a combine. Now, I think some provision might be made in this bill that where a registrar discovers that a combine exists, and that this combine is subsidized by the government in order that it may exist, the government should cancel the subsidy or any unpaid portion of it during the year in which the discovery was made. That is only a suggestion, but as to the fact whether this is a combine or not the Ottawa Journal goes along for two columns and gives the history of two cases. It connects me very thoroughly with one and ends up by saying that I should be the last person, or words to that effect, to complain because the Canadian Press did eventually grant a franchise to a paper that I promoted and own. The facts are I was a director of the Windsor Telegram, that the Windsor Telegram invested in buildings, plant, machinery and paper $167,000, put a paper on the street, and then asked the Canadian Press for a franchise. The only connection I ever had with that, except writing a few letters, was to appear for five minufes before the Canadian Press at the city of Toronto. They said: ''It is all very fine. There is one paper in your border cities of sixty thousand. If you stand the gaff long enough we will probably give you a franchise next September." We carried along our paper without any telegraphic news whatever because the Canadian Press absolutely controls the telegraphic news of this country. It also has an agreement with the Associated Press, and it is impossible for any newspaper in this country to get any telegraphic news without the Canadian Press service. They say in this article, and have said before, that they do not prevent anyone from starting a daily newspaper. Quite right. Mr. Herman could come into the city of Ottawa and invest a million dollars in plant, land, buildings and machinery, and put a daily newspaper on the streets of Ottawa, but he would have no telegraphic news in it. He would have no news of the proceedings of the legislatures. It is true that he could put a special reporter here, but he would have no news from any other part of Canada unless he owned a franchise now controlled absolutely by the Canadian Press, which is controlled in this city by three men, not five, as is stated in this article,-because the Citizen owns two franchises, the Journal owns two, and the French paper one.

Combines
Now that is the situation. If that is a com-, bine, if the people of this country are willing to pay that combine $58,000 a year so that it will exist, we should know whether a newspaper owner or any number of men who wish to start another daily paper in any part of this country cannot have the telegraphic news.
I suggest humbly that it is possible somewhere in this act to take care of a situation such as that. I believe personally that the combine does exist. I believe that it is not for the benefit of the public that it exists. I do not for one moment criticise the service rendered by the Canadian Press. The statement in this article is absolutely correct, that every report sent out by the Canadian Press is accurate. There has been no politics of any description in the reports sent out. I am not attempting to criticise the newspaper men, but I do criticise the men who control these franchises and I say it is to the detriment of the general public of this country that such a situation exists, and that we should cease subsidizing them and perhaps cease allowing them to gather their news over the telegraphic lines owned by the people of this country.

speechtext: I would point out to my hon. friend that the government is not seeking, in connection with this bill, the right to make any more appointments than have been thought advisable, for example, in the case of royal commissions empowered to investigate different subjects. On section 22-Distribution of report:

Is it the intention that the
report shall be available to anybody who wishes to get it? If so why should it be left to the minister to furnish copies? Under section 19 the proceedings of the registrar and commissioner are to be conducted in private, but the minister may order any portion of those proceedings to be conducted in public. When it comes to the report it is provided that a newspaper or any person can get it only if the minister so directs. I do not 6ee any necessity at all for that precaution. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There again, Mr. Chairman, I would feel that there is a responsibility with the minister which he may be expected to exercise in accordance with what was in the public interest. I can conceive of some cases where, perhaps, it would be the part of wisdom for a minister to withhold a report. But he would be responsible to parliament for his action in so doing; he would have to give the reason for having refused to make a report public. In fact I can conceive of cases where the commissioners might, after having gone into a matter very fully, give it as their opinion that it was inadvisable that the report should be made public. Therefore I think, discre-

Combines
tion should be left with the minister in that regard. Personally I am rather sympathetic with the point of view of my hon. friends opposite that everything should be made public; but let me point out again that the government, in this legislation, has sought to avoid what some hon. gentlemen have pointed out as a possible danger-too much interference with business and subjecting private businesses to an amount of publicity that might bring about a possible injury. The government is sincere it its desire to not prejudice a private interest if that can possibly be avoided in the carrying out of this legislation. I think, probably, it is wise to leave with the minister discretion as to the amount of publicity that is to be given to a report.

I do not know that I can agree with my right hon. friend there. I quite appreciate that the earlier stages of the inquiry should be private; but when you have once found that there was something to inquire into, and when a commissioner goes into the matter and hears the evidence and a report is made, surely what I suggest is not going to hurt the firm or person investigated. If the report is unfavourable why should not the public have a right to know the result of the proceedings for which they are paying? As the bill stands at present the whole thing is absolutely private from beginning to end and even the report can be withheld unless the minister chooses to say it can be made public. Not one single step to be taken under the provisions of this bill can be made public except with the minister's authority. Even when the country has paid for the investigation and the report arising out of it is ready that report cannot be obtained except with the minister's permission. The newspapers of the country cannot get the report, the newspapers cannot even be represented at the investigation unless, forsooth a minister of the Crown says so. I am absolutely in accord with the views of the Prime Minister as to the earlier stages of the investigation: I do not think it would be fair to a company, when the matter is being first investigated, that the press and public should know all about it. But when the registrar is of the opinion that there is something to be investigated, and when a commissioner is appointed to take that investigation in hand, why in the world should not the proceedings of that court be open to the public and the press just as readily as the proceedings of any court of justice. Whether the Prime Minister will agree with me in that I do not know; but to maintain, that after a report
has been made, the press and the public are not entitled to a copy of it unless some minister says they may have it, seems to me extraordinary. I have heard nothing from the Prime Minister which justifies that. Let me repeat:	If the report
whitewashes a suggested combine surely to goodness they would want it made public and they, or anybody else, ought to be able to get a copy of the report. On the other hand, if the report finds there has been a combine why put it in the hands of any minister to hush the whole thing up if he wants to? Surely it is in the public interest that the matter should then be made public? What is the good of this bill if the whole thing can be kept from the public? I am not saying the minister will do this, I hardly believe he wants to do it, but why give him this power? The proceedings having reached the stage where the alleged combine is being investigated, the parties concerned being represented by counsel if necessary, I cannot see why they should not then be just a3 public as in any court of justice. However, if the Prime Minister does not think that procedure is correct I do trust he will accede to the suggestion that at least those interested, including the public and the press, may get a copy of the report when that report is made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think the
word "may" is, to all intents and purposes, equivalent to the word "shall" with this one possible difference; that if you insert the word "shall" you leave no discretion whatever for the holding back of an individual report. You compel every report to be published, regardless altogether of what the circumstances may be. In the event of any report being withheld, the minister is responsible. I have not the slightest objection, if my hon. friend wishes, to move to insert the word "shall" in place of the word "may". The only reason the government has used the language which appears in this bill is the one I have given, an endeavour to have caution exercised in respect of any matters which are likely to be of concern to private business, so as to interfere as little as possible with private business. I feel certain that the minister administering the act would take advantage of the word "may" to give publicity to reports which had been received. If he is given that permission I think that is almost sufficient guarantee that he will exercise it. unless there is exceptional reason for not doing so.	[DOT]

But my point is as to the words "if the minister so directs". The section reads:
A copy of any report may, if the minister so directs, be sent free of charge to any person.
And so on. My suggestion is that it should be amended so as to read:
A copy of any report shall be available and free to any j erson and to anjr newspaper in Canada.

As to a case in which the report is against the concern being investigated. as referred to a few moments ago, I would like to ask a question. Considering that the minister has no authority to assess the penalties, or to finally determine, in a real court of justice, the actual guilt for penalty assessing purposes, does the hon. member think it would be in accordance with British justice that the report should be heralded through the country at all times broadcast to the world that one single individual, acting as a commissioner, had expressed to the minister his best judgment that a serious situation existed, that should be sent on-
This is a speech, not a question.
No, it is a question.
I will answer it, if the minister will give me a chance.

Does the hon. member
think it would be in accordance with British justice to send a man to trial with that cloud hanging over him? Would that not rather be a proper thing for the attorney general of the province or the Solicitor General to deal with in sending the case on for determination.

I do not think the question is at all troublesome. Have you not exactly the same state of affairs in a preliminary investigation in any criminal court? Many people are prosecuted in the police court. An investigation takes place there. If the magistrate thinks there is sufficient evidence to place the party on trial, the proceedings in the police court are public, and the party is sent up for trial. At the same time these parties are sometimes found to be innocent. After you have had your preliminary investigation, and this registrar, who has the status of a deputy minister, a fairly responsible man, comes to the [Mr. Bovs.l
conclusion that there is something to investigate, you then go further and your commissioner, another high-priced and capable man, investigates the matter. Both sides are heard. He thinks there is a combine. Do you not think it is time the public knew something about it?

I am entirely willing to
accept the hon. member's view.

I am delighted I have made
some impression on the minister. I was trying to answer his question. I cannot see anything terrible about what the minister has suggested. I did not hear all the discussion yesterday. I was more pleasantly engaged.
Where?

Read the papers and you
will find out. I understood the suggestion was
there was to be so much light thrown upon this, and it was to be exposed to the sun. Now, I find the whole thing is to be in camera, unless the minister otherwise directs. Coming back to my suggestion-and I make it for the last time-I say that this clause should be amended so that when we reach the last stage of a double investigation no matter what the report is, any newspaper or any individual should be permitted to get a copy of the report if they want it.
Then the bill goes on and provides that the proceedings should be sent to the attorney general, and he should institute proceedings and if he does not do so in three months, the department at Ottawa takes it in hand, and we have a further investigation. It seems to me the provisions of the bill are useless if, when you go through the entire process, the public can not even get a copy of the report unless the minister says so.

I think it would be bettei if the House did not pass this bill at all. The committee has carried twenty one clauses, and we are never going to get anywhere in regulating the trusts and combines with this bill. The result of this bill, if it passes, will simply mean a lot of party politics. The registrar and the commissioner, when appointed, will be under the control of a minister of the Crown, While he may be a good minister, he is still a politician, and he will have to deal with the matter of regulation of trusts and combines. This bill provides for a private or star chamber inquiry, and we are not going to get anywhere against the powerful influence of the shipping combine and other trusts, the banking institutions, the gTeat manufacturers' association, and all the rest of these trusts and combines. We have had on and off the

Combines
statute books for thirty years various legislation dealing with this problem, and we have never got anywhere in solving it. We have not been able to accomplish anything for the working classes in the way of bringing down the cost of living. I listened to the Minister of Labour yesterday and to-day,^ and I may say that the more I look into this bill the more I am convinced that it is simply fashioned after the style of the Board of Commerce Act of 1919. The registrar will be a politician, and the commissioner will be a politician; one reports to the other, and the other reports to the minister, and then you have got to the end of the first circle. They have to go to the minister and get permission to go further. The proceeding is not conducted as a court would be conducted at all. They had the same legislation in the United States twenty years ago, but they went further, and as I said yesterday the grand jury system was then adopted. Our Board of Commerce Act was based on the same principle as the United States Federal Trade Commission. They did not get anywhere. What has been the result in Chicago under the grand jury system? They had the great motor combines and the oil combines indicted. These gigantic combines are located at the foot of lake Michigan, in the city of Chicago. The grand jury sat and Judge Landis fined the Standard Oil fifty million dollars.
I urge that we take this question out of party politics, and leave it to the grand juries in the different centres of population throughout Canada. In that way we would relieve the government of a great burden. I do not think it is fair to ask the government of Canada, whether this government or their successors, to deal with this matter. The Ministers of the Crown are too busy to attend to it. It is not fair to ask them to take hold of a matter like this, and the country does not expect the government to do the impossible. I think it would be far better if the minister would consider whether he would not, at the end of this bill insert a provision vesting in the grand juries throughout the country the power to deal with this question. There are judicial and national questions and they deal with economic matters. We must be fair to capital on the one side, and to everybody concerned in trade and commerce. You cannot deal with the matter properly if you are going to handle it as a political question instead of as an economic one. You must be fair to the mergers and trusts in that respect, because some of them have been doing good work; some of them have been effecting economies in many spheres of activity.
The majority, however, have not, and they should be under some form of public control. Railway transportation interests are under the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners ; they are not under the control of a registrar or of a commission, and there is a suggestion to give that commission increased powers and to put transportation on the ocean and the Great Lakes under its control. If that board can deal with matters like that which are of a national character, surely grand juries can handle the trusts and combines better. They know local conditions and the judges and juries have the time, which a busy minister of the Crown has not, to study the problems. I do not think it is fair to a minister of the Crown on the opposite side, because ministers are loaded up with work, that he should have to assume this additional burden. I would not ask the Prime Minister to do so. The grand jury is a judicial body which can handle this question, it has the time and machinery to handle it, and it is the only body in the Dominion of Canada that can properly handle this question. Under the old Combines Act, 1910, there was only one inquiry, that into the United Shoe Machinery Company; the minister said that from 1908 to 1923 there was only this one inquiry.
Conditions are continually changing in Canada. I hope tl*e government will succeed under this legislation, but I doubt very much if they are going to succeed. I do not doubt their sincerity; I do not doubt the sincerity of the Prime Minister in introducing this legislation; I give him credit for bringing this legislation before parliament. I will be glad to see him bring about some results; but on the one hand, in these days of stress and strain, we must not forget that the capitalists have some rights and, on the other hand, the consumers must come in somewhere. Therefore, I think the courts are better fitted for this work than ministers of the Crown, and registrars and commissioners appointed as they no doubt will be under party politics. We should take this whole question out of party politics to get results.

The minister may feel that the case is one which should go on

immediately to the courts as the combine is of a character that should be prosecuted. He might wish to reserve for the time being, to place in the hands of the attorney general of the province or the Solicitor General who might be prosecuting the combine, the evidence and the report made on the evidence. It might be to the public interest that all those facts should not be disclosed before the case comes to trial. That discretion should be left with the minister. At all events. I would say to my hon. friend that I think that is a clause which might be permitted to stand as it is, at least, until the legislation is given a trial, and if experience shows that it is wise to make it mandatory rather than permissive, we can have it amended at a subsequent session.
Mr. I'ORKE' I am rather in sympathy with the remarks of the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Boys). speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

I might point out to my hon. friend that his remarks would have great force and weight and I would agree with him wholly, were it the circumstance that the minister is not responsible to parliament for everything that he does. But when members of the committee recall that with respect to every action of a minister, either in giving out a report, or in withholding it, he is accountable to parliament, and that any hon. member may call for any report that has been made, may demand from the minister in the presence of his fellow members, an explanation of why that report was not made public at a particular time, with that thought in mind, having regard to the unforeseen nature of the circumstances of different cases and what the public interest at the moment may render most desirable,

I think it is better not to take away the discretionary power of the minister. I think a minister will seek at all times to further what he believes to be the public interest. I cannot conceive of any minister, unless he is heading straight to destruction, both for himself and for his government, trying to take a course that will be other than in the public interest and one that he can defend on the floor of parhament. That is 'my reason for thinking that, on the whole, it is wiser to leave with the minister the discretion as to the time, at any rate, of giving out a report that may be made.
Just let us see how far we are really going in this legislation -towards enabling the whole of the matter to be turned into a matter of party political exigency, that and nothing else.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend this question when he speaks about turning the whole matter into a matter of party political exigency? Is that the point of view from which he would administer the legislation? If not, why should he impute a different motive to anyone else?

I cannot see any other reason from the manner in which the bill -is drawn. In the first instance, my hon. friend is perfectly right. He is going into this question of a combine, and he does not know whether there is anything in it or not. He puts a man, in whom he is supposed to have trust and confidence-or else he would not appoint him-in a position for the purpose of finding out whether the prima facie case is such that it is clear that a combine exists. It is quite right that that should be all private. Nobody is arguing that that should be made public. That is the first proceeding. The second proceeding is this, that my hon. friend turns around and this particular concern over here is turned inside out, and that particular concern over there is turned inside out for the purpose of finding out whether the commissioner or the registrar was correct or not in his views. Those people are, in effect, on trial and they ought to be. I am not quarrelling with that at all. They are undergoing a preliminary investigation, and they are undergoing a preliminary investigation at the hands of the person that my hon. friend again has to have confidence in or he ought not to appoint him, for the purpose of finding out whether or not they are guilty of an offence. On top of all that, money is being spent. The investigation here and the investigation there are costing the country money, for experts,

Combines
commissioners, time, evidence and the like. The result is a result from which further criminal proceedings are to start or not to start, just exactly the same as in the case of a preliminary investigation. The crime is certainly no graver than are crimes that are covered by preliminary investigations. These preliminary investigations are held under the laws passed by this House. They are public; they relate to far more serious offences, such as the improper publication of the opinion of a magistrate that the committal should be made, and they do far more harm than any mere trade offence can do. And there are further investigations that are not surrounded with as many safeguards as we have here. I ask my hon. friend why there should be the difference, unless there is to be political favouritism or favouritism of some other kind. A concern over here, let us say, is being investigated. The minister may not like the colour of the man's hair or the kind of business he carried on, and he makes the report public. Another concern is being investigated at the same time; the minister likes the man and thinks his business is all right; and there is no publicity in that case. The one is taken and the other is left. If my hon. friend wants to have something like unifrom treatment of companies and wishes to see justice in the administration of the act, there should be no room for such favouritism. The minister should take his stand openly in regard to either course. He may be right or wrong in both, but the public surely have a right to know what the facte are. We have criticized this bill on the ground that it is going to take us nowhere. Surely my hon. friend must see the force of these criticisms, if the whole thing is to be left to the possibility of being tied up in secrecy. My hon. friend suggests that the matter should be kept quiet until the attorney general knows about it. Why? Why should it be kept quiet before the attorney general knows about it any more than any other crime under the statute? What possible harm can come of publicity? I think my hon. friend on further consideration should have that clause so amended as to provide that the public shall have the second report when it is made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member starts on the assumption that the minister who is to administer the act will not make the reports public; I think I am equally entitled to assume that he will make all reports public. It is from that point of view that the government is proceeding, namely, that the reports will all be made public unless there is some very special reason why publicity should not be given to a particular report at a particular time. I think that any minister who would refuse to make a report would incur a great responsibility. The minister in charge would be very careful in exercising that right in view of that responsibility.
I have in mind a matter that is the subject of inquiry at the present moment,-the question of freight rates on the Great Lakes. The government had a preliminary investigation made of that matter and a report was presented by the investigator. I believe the whole report has been substantiated under a royal commission which had power to put parties under oath. An effort was made on the part of interests concerned to secure a copy of the report before they were brought to the position where they would have to appear before the commission for investigation. The government refused to make the report public, believing that it was in the public interest that the information gathered in that way should be handed over to the commission that was to make inquiry into the matter and be used by the commission in such a manner as would best serve the public interest. The government, I think, was wise in withholding the report from publication at the time; and I can conceive of cases under this act where, a group of interests having associated themselves, are acting in a manner detrimental to the interest of the public, information is obtained and a report submitted which is so strong that the government intends then to proceed to prosecution of the combine concerned. It might in such cases be very much in the interest of the public to withhold the report of the evidence on which the decision to prosecute is based, until such time as the combine itself has been investigated in a court of law in the regular way. This is a matter that can be determined only in the light of each case as it arises. I am entirely with my hon. friends opposite in this regard,-I think that wherever it is possible, and there is reasonable ground for believing that no just interest will suffer, the fullest publicity should be gi^en to all proceedings under the act.
My right hon. friend is with us, but he will not accede to our request.

You might have a report recommending a prosecution or stating that a combine existed, and if the minister were a man susceptible to influence, and if he were so influenced, the work of the whole investigation could be frustrated merely by a word from him.
